title: The buffalo in the mud, and two vowels made behind a grin

slides.heading: One letter, two vowels, and a piece of furniture
body: One consonant, and a costly one to get wrong.
Two vowels English cannot make.
And something that turns up only to prop a vowel up.

slides.heading: You already know how it sounds in a word
body: It lives at the harbour, so it is low class.
Every tone rule you have applies to it **unchanged**.
The new thing about it is not a sound. It is a direction.

slides.heading: Pen and paper, and today it is the point
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Today's letter differs from a known one **only by direction**.
The eye cannot see it. The hand can.

slides.heading: The buffalo
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **water buffalo**.
A k with a gust of breath. The palm moves.

slides.heading: The one nobody quite owns
body: It works the vegetable plots behind the harbour.
Nobody agrees whose it is, and it does not seem to mind.
At midday it takes itself down to the mud.

slides.heading: The sound it makes going in
body: One enormous breath out as it lowers itself in.
Caked, cool and completely calm.
And it throws its head **back over its shoulder**.

slides.heading: The buffalo's letter
body: A rounded bowl, the same one you have seen before.
The head curls **outward and back**, not tucked inside.

slides.heading: This is the pair you were warned about
body: Lesson one promised you a pair that differs only by head direction.
**This is it.** The child's letter and the buffalo's letter.
Same bowl. One head tucked in, one thrown back.

slides.heading: And what it costs to get it wrong
body: The child is in the market: **mid class**. The buffalo is at the harbour: **low class**.
Curl the head the wrong way and the letter changes district.
District changes class, class changes tone, tone changes the word.

slides.heading: Write it, and write the other one beside it
body: Write the child's letter first. Head inside, clockwise.
Then the buffalo beside it. Head **outward and back**.
Alternate them. You are training the wrist, not the eye.

slides.prompt: The child's letter and the buffalo's letter are the same bowl. Name the difference, and say what it costs you to get it wrong.

answers: The head: tucked in and clockwise, against thrown back the other way.
Wrong way round moves it from the market to the harbour.
Mid class becomes low class, and the tone follows.

slides.heading: Back up to the roof, where somebody else lives
body: Back to the roof, where a vowel written above lodges.
There is a second lodger up there.
His sound does not exist in English. That is new.

slides.heading: The other one upstairs
body: The name means **other**, or another.
There is no English word for this sound. There is no point looking.
Wide grin, hold it, then try to say oo through it.

slides.heading: Unless you happen to speak Swedish
body: Swedish speakers already own this sound: the u in **hus**, in **ut**.
Pull the lips back rather than pushing them forward.
English has nothing here. Swedish does.

slides.heading: Both of him, and you know this trick
body: Two of him: short and long, same sound.
**More on the mark means longer.** Third time you have met this.
Short: a small ring on top. Long: a second upright beside it.

slides.heading: The short one, in a word
body: The mouse's letter, short grin vowel above, chicken's letter closing it.
**นึก** — to call something to mind.
Short: over before it settles.

slides.heading: Write them both
body: Always above a consonant. Never alone.
Put them over the letter you just learned.
Say the whole syllable, grin and all.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Buffalo, long grin vowel above, mouse closing it.
**Say it aloud before you turn it over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **คืน** — to return, and also a night.

slides.heading: The word for hand has a letter you have never met
body: A vowel written **above** needs something beneath it to close the syllable.
When a final consonant closes it, there is something.
When the syllable ends bare, a **prop** is written in.

slides.heading: And one you will use constantly
body: **คือ** — the word for *is*.
The test is not the sound.
**Does a consonant follow the vowel?** If not, the prop goes in.

slides.prompt: Of a syllable reading khuue, one reading khuuen and one reading muue, one needs no prop. Which, and why?

answers: The one closing on a final consonant stands on its own.
The two that end bare are both written with the prop.
The test is never the sound. It is whether a consonant follows.

slides.heading: One last word, and it is a big one
body: Buffalo, then the mouse's letter, and nothing written between.
Thai leaves a short vowel out there.
**Say it before you turn it over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **คน** — a person.

slides.heading: One band down, and the shape of things
body: Thirteen letters, nine vowels.
A stroke direction can carry a class, and now you have met one.
From here: more letters, the same machine.
